claims.text: Thermal treatments induce a controllable degree of short-range chemical order in HfNbTaTiZr.
Short-range chemical ordering creates localized lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
SRO-induced lattice distortions alter dislocation mobility.
SRO-induced lattice distortions alter the elastic lattice response.

SRO-induced distortions provide a unified explanation for high-temperature creep, cold-rolling microhardness evolution, temperature-dependent elastic moduli, and thermal-expansion-related internal stresses.
High-temperature solution treatment produces a homogenized, single-phase, disordered HfNbTaTiZr solid solution.
Rapid quenching from the homogenization temperature maintains a relatively random state without significant SRO.
Aging HfNbTaTiZr at 600–800 °C promotes measurable SRO formation.
Local distortions associated with SRO hinder dislocation motion.
The impediment of dislocation motion by SRO enhances creep resistance and work hardening.
SRO-associated lattice distortions alter lattice stiffness.
SRO-associated distortions modify the effective thermal expansion behavior and thereby contribute to thermal stresses during cooling or interaction with composite phases.
Relative to the quenched baseline, aged specimens will exhibit increased creep resistance at approximately 1250 °C.
Relative to the quenched baseline, aged specimens will exhibit higher microhardness after an identical amount of cold rolling.
Relative to the quenched baseline, aged specimens will exhibit modified, likely higher and more temperature-sensitive, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K.
Relative to the quenched baseline, aged specimens will exhibit altered thermal expansion and measurable internal stresses during cooling.
The SRO effect can remain apparent during creep testing at 1250 °C despite being introduced by aging at 600–800 °C.
Quenched and 700 °C-aged specimens should be compared under identical creep, cold-rolling, modulus, and cooling conditions.
The proposed SRO mechanism is falsified if the measured property differences are not statistically significant or do not correlate with measured SRO.
